data.hypothesis: The valid 32x8 direct-global mapping averaged 3.004 μs versus 3.278 μs for the flattened candidate and 3.494 μs for the baseline, but those measurements do not isolate a cause. This experiment retains 256 threads per block and contiguous-x warp lanes while changing the tile to 64x4: each CTA covers complete x rows and two warps per row instead of splitting each row across CTAs. This tests whether that mapping changes full-run latency; no speedup is assumed.

memory_lessons.applicability: Observed event latencies for this fixed 64³ stencil and the supplied measurement protocol; they do not establish why the mappings differ.
memory_lessons.claim: The baseline was correct at 3.494 μs mean; the flattened direct-global program was correct at 3.278 μs, and the 32x8 direct-global program was correct at 3.004 μs. The 32x8 candidate is the fastest observed among these, but the results do not prove a causal mapping benefit.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure and oracle-check the 64x4 full-row mapping using the same full-run event-latency protocol.

data.notes: Proposes a 64x4 block and a 1x16x64 grid (1024 blocks, 256 threads per block). The direct kernel has no shared-memory use or block-wide barriers, writes one output for each of the 64³ points, and is launched once per call. The eight y-neighbor rows each apply the baseline's my-1 halo adjustment independently. Correctness and latency remain for controller evaluation.
transformations: Replace shared-memory staging and block-wide barriers with direct-global neighbor loads and one output per thread.
Use a 64x4 block and a 1x16x64 grid, retaining 256 threads per block and mapping warp lanes to contiguous x elements.
Unroll the four positive/negative y-neighbor pairs and apply the baseline my-1 halo adjustment to every offset independently.
Write all 64³ outputs from the current A input on every call with one launch and no additional allocation.
